plan.topic: Tirzepatide diarrhea: is it normal, and when does it usually ease? Label rates per dose vs placebo, and the label's timing during dose increases
plan.angle: Tirzepatide diarrhoea Short, tight arm. Sentence 1 (≤14 words) names tirzepatide and says diarrhoea is a common side effect in the trials. By 6 s: the Zepbound label rate per dose vs placebo over the trial period (one label only, named on the card), then 'in the trials it was more common during dose increases', in label wording, framed as a trial pattern, not a prediction. Tips (untagged): sip fluids unless you've been told to limit them; ask a pharmacist before any anti-diarrhoea product. When to get help: signs of dehydration (the label links it to kidney problems), or diarrhoea that's severe or won't settle. Emergency card: severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting → stop and call your healthcare provider (label wording). Then: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Then 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, the Exp F line and the closing line. Title: 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Diarrhea: Will It Ease? #shorts'. Post note: related-video target is the 11-09 Diarrhea long video.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Diarrhea: Will It Go Away? #shorts
plan.why: Felt symptom in the proven calm 'Is this normal?' format. No Short has covered diarrhea yet, and it funnels to the 11-09 Diarrhea long video. | fact-check: This is a proven body-worry format with a new fact (per-dose label rates), so the topic is approved. Two safety problems need fixing. (1) 'Severe stomach pain that won't go away' is the label's pancreatitis wording, and for pancreatitis the label says to stop and call your healthcare provider. So the don't-stop line must be scoped ('For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs…'), and the pancreatitis card must name its trigger and the stop-and-call instruction. (2) Use one label for the rates and say which one. The Zepbound (weight) and Mounjaro (T2D) tables differ, so don't mix them, and name placebo plus the timeframe. The dehydration red flag should use the label's wording that dehydration from vomiting and diarrhoea has been linked to kidney problems. The pharmacist line before any anti-diarrhoea product is fine and gets no source tag. Diarrhoea timing must stay the label's own wording ('during dose escalation'/'dose increases') as a trial pattern, with no promise about when it will stop. Add when to see a doctor: diarrhoea that's severe or won't settle, or signs of dehydration such as dizziness or very little urine. Title: avoid promising 'Will It Go Away?' as a yes. The script must answer with the hedge ('often eases, per the trials, but not for everyone').

package.title: Tirzepatide and Diarrhea: Is It Normal? #shorts
package.description:
Tirzepatide diarrhea: 19–23 in 100 on tirzepatide vs about 8 in 100 on placebo in 72-week trials in adults with overweight or obesity. In trials, most cases showed up during dose increases and tended to ease over time, though not for everyone.
Severe, won't settle, dizzy, or barely urinating? Call your doctor. The label links dehydration to kidney problems.
Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, may be pancreatitis: stop and call your healthcare provider right away.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
#Tirzepatide #GLP1 #SideEffects
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.cta: Spoken close (08:00 slot, Exp F still running): "We answer one tirzepatide question from the research every day. Subscribe if that helps. Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description." POST NOTE for the owner: the related-video target is the 11-09 Tirzepatide Diarrhea long video. WORD COUNT: 157 spoken words, or 160 if the hyphenated words (seventy-two, twenty-three, anti-diarrheals) count as two. The standard arm is 135–160, so this is inside the range either way. FACT-CHECK FIXES APPLIED: (1) s6 now says "right away" in the narration, list item 4 and the on-screen text. (2) s3 uses the label-close wording "most cases showed up during dose increases, and tended to ease over time", and its on-screen text is "Trial pattern: most during dose increases". (3) s2's on-screen text is now "Tirzepatide 5–15 mg: 19–23 in 100 vs ~8 on placebo", and the attribution line is kept. The narration now speaks the measure ("Diarrhea") and "across tirzepatide doses" so the muted test works both ways. Placebo is spoken as "eight", which matches the PI's 8%. (4) The zep_mg URL is changed to https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-us-mg.pdf. ACTION BEFORE PUBLISHING: confirm the revision date printed on the Medication Guide PDF and add it to the zep_mg source entry. Don't assume 28 Aug 2026; that date is confirmed only for the PI. TRIM NOTES: s1 went from "On tirzepatide and dealing with diarrhea?" to "On tirzepatide with diarrhea?", s4 now says "anti-diarrheals", and the s5 checklist is tightened, all to stay under 160 words after the fixes. Captions: keep "5–15 mg", "19–23" and "~8" whole on one card, never split.

factcheck.summary: I checked every number against the live Zepbound PI (Revised 8/2026), and they're right. Table 1 (Study 1 and Study 2 pooled, 72 weeks, adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition) lists diarrhea at 19% on 5 mg, 21% on 10 mg and 23% on 15 mg, against 8% on placebo. So placebo is 8%, and "about eight" is fine. The PI says "The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time." That supports s3 and the title's "Will It Ease?". The PI also says most acute kidney injury cases happened in people with GI reactions that led to dehydration, which supports s5. The Medication Guide tells people to stop and call their healthcare provider "right away" for severe stomach-area pain that will not go away, with or without vomiting. The safety lines, their order and the scoped don't-stop line are all correct, and so are the Exp F and closing lines. I found only wording fixes: s6 drops the label's urgency word, s3 could follow the label more closely, the s2 stat card should label both groups for muted viewers, and the zep_mg source should point to the Medication Guide's own document.
